newsitem.title: UK: Voters find two-dimensional politicians suit them.
newsitem.headline: Voters find two-dimensional politicians suit them.

text.p: Commentators may be right when they complain that politicians look like two-dimensional cardboard cut-outs, researchers said on Wednesday.
They said people use a completely separate, two-point scale when assessing politicians as opposed to other people.

Most people use a fairly complex gauge of personality when deciding what someone is like, or when assessing themselves. But when deciding who to vote for the rules get simplified, said Gian Vittorio Caprara and Caludio Barbaranelli of the University of Rome, who worked with Philip Zimbardo of Stanford University in California.
"We found that, when people judge the personality traits of politicians, they use only two or three factors," they wrote in a letter to the scientific journal Nature..

Psychologists use five different factors to evaluate personality -- energy and extroversion, agreeableness and friendliness, conscientiousness, emotional stability versus neuroticism and intellect and openness to experience.
Caprara's group asked 2,000 Italians to evaluate the personalities of either leading politicians, celebrities or themselves.
"Judgments were made from a list of 25 adjectives that are markers of the five-factor model," they wrote.
When judging themselves, nearly everyone used all five factors. The same applied when they were asked to assess skiing hero Alberto Tomba and television personality Pippo Baudo.
But new factors were used when evaluating politicians Silvio Berlusconi and Roman Prodi during a recent election campaign.
"Personality factors that are normally independent -- such as energy and openness -- were highly correlated in a more simplified view of personality," they wrote.
Zimbardo reproduced the effect when he tested 195 university students in the United States.
He said simplifying the process was evidently an efficient strategy for combating information overload.
"Doing so helps them (voters) decide how to cast their vote," he concluded, saying savvy politicians could take advantage of the effect.

"It could help political candidates if they used this psychological profile earlier in their campaign to determine the kind of personality packaging that voters were tying up on them," he said by telephone.
